title: HTML: Structure, Semantics and Forms
sub: Write documents that browsers, screen readers and servers all understand: the skeleton, the parse tree, semantic elements, links, images, tables and forms that send data
goals: Write a correct document skeleton and say what every line of the head does
Predict the DOM tree the parser builds, including how it repairs bad nesting, and check it in Elements
Mark up a page with landmarks, an ordered heading outline, lists, links, images and an accessible data table
Build forms with the right input types, labels and built-in validation, and say exactly what the browser sends for GET, POST and multipart
Use id, class and data-* attributes for their separate jobs and apply the core accessibility rules
Choose between classic, defer, async and module scripts

blocks.text: HTML is the part of a page that carries meaning: this is a heading, this is a list of devices, this is a field for an IP address, this button sends the form. Browsers render it, screen readers speak it, search engines index it, Safari's Reader view reformats it, and servers receive what its forms send. In this chapter you will write the skeleton of a document and learn what each line does, watch the parser turn markup into a tree and repair your mistakes, mark up a router status page with semantic elements, build an accessible device table, and build a device-registration form whose every byte you can trace to the request the browser sends.

Keep `python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1` running in `~/lab/web` from [How the Web Works](#web-intro/first-page). Anything you write in a playground here you can also save as a file in that folder and open at `http://localhost:8000/`, with real DevTools.
The skeleton of a document
Every page you write should start from this skeleton. Save it as `~/lab/web/status.html`:

blocks.text: The doctype is a switch, not a version number. Every document the browser builds has a `compatMode`: `CSS1Compat` is standards mode, `BackCompat` is quirks mode. `DOMParser` (you will use it properly in [XML and Friends](#xml)) parses a string into a separate document, which lets you test both cases:

blocks.title: Garbled characters mean an encoding mismatch

blocks.text: If `café` shows up as `cafÃ©`, UTF-8 bytes were decoded as Windows-1252. The browser takes the charset from the `Content-Type` header first and from `<meta charset>` second. `python3 -m http.server` sends plain `Content-type: text/html` with no charset, so the meta tag decides; leave it out and the browser guesses. Save files as UTF-8 and always include the meta tag as the first child of `<head>`.

blocks.name: <meta name="viewport">
blocks.sum: Tell mobile browsers to use the device's real width as the layout width, so responsive CSS works.

how.text: Phones were designed when most sites assumed a desktop screen, so mobile browsers lay a page out on a virtual **layout viewport** about 980 CSS pixels wide and then shrink it to fit the screen. Your text becomes tiny and media queries such as `(max-width: 600px)` never match. `width=device-width` sets the layout viewport to the device width in CSS pixels (about 390 to 440 on current iPhones), and `initial-scale=1` starts at 100 % zoom.

Do not add `maximum-scale=1` or `user-scalable=no`: they stop people with poor eyesight from zooming, and current iOS ignores them anyway. The tag has no effect in desktop browsers; test it in Safari's Responsive Design Mode, Chrome's device toolbar or on your phone over your LAN.

examples.desc: In the Console of a page, read the viewport width the CSS sees
Find the pages in your web folder that are missing the tag

gotchas: Without this tag your page looks fine on the Mac and microscopic on the phone, which is why it belongs in every skeleton.

blocks.text: Optional tags

The parser inserts ``, `` and `` when you leave them out, and the end tags `

`, ``, ``, `` and several others are optional by the specification. That is why sloppy pages still work:

blocks.code:
const doc = new DOMParser().parseFromString('Lab

hi', 'text/html'); console.log(doc.documentElement.outerHTML);

blocks.text: Write them anyway. Explicit structure is easier to read, to diff and to debug, and the next section shows the cases where the parser's guess differs from yours.
Elements, tags and attributes

Three words get mixed up constantly. A **tag** is the syntax in the source: `` is a start tag, `` an end tag. An **element** is the node the parser builds from them, with its contents. An **attribute** is a `name="value"` pair on a start tag that configures the element.

tokens.exp: start tag opens: the element name is a (anchor, a link)
attribute: where the link goes, a relative URL
attribute: a class name for CSS and scripts to hook onto
attribute: tells assistive technology this link is the current page
content: the link text, what users see and screen readers announce

blocks.text: The rules of the syntax:

items.text: **Names are case-insensitive**: `<A HREF>` works, but write lower case, as everyone does.
**Quote attribute values** with double quotes. Unquoted values work only without spaces or the characters `" ' = < >` and backtick, so quoting always is simpler.

**Boolean attributes** are true when present, whatever their value: `disabled`, `required`, `checked`, `selected`, `hidden`, `multiple`, `readonly`. `disabled="false"` is still disabled. To turn one off, remove the attribute.

**Void elements** have no content and no end tag: `area base br col embed hr img input link meta source track wbr`. A trailing slash (`
`) is allowed and ignored.

**Elements nest**; close them in reverse order of opening: `

...

`.

blocks.title: A self-closing slash does nothing on normal elements

blocks.text:
HTML is not XML. `
` is read as `
`, with the slash ignored, so the div stays open and swallows everything after it: `
text aftermore` parses as `
text aftermore
`. Only void elements can be "self-closing", and they do not need the slash. SVG and MathML inside HTML are the exception: there, `` really closes.
What may go inside what

Every element has a **content model**, the list of things allowed inside it. Two categories cover most cases. **Flow content** is nearly everything that can appear in `<body>`. **Phrasing content** is text and the inline elements that mark up text: `a`, `em`, `strong`, `code`, `span`, `img`, `input`, `button`, `label`, `time`, `abbr`, `br`. The rules you will hit first:

items.text:
`

`, `

`-`

`, `
`<ul>` and `<ol>` contain only `<li>` (plus `<script>` and `<template>`). `<dl>` contains `<dt>`/`<dd>` groups.
`<a>` is **transparent**: it may contain whatever its parent may contain, so a link can wrap a whole card, but it must not contain another link or a button.
Tables have a fixed structure: `caption`, `colgroup`, `thead`, `tbody`, `tfoot`, `tr`, `th`, `td`, in that order.

blocks.text: **Block** and **inline** are not HTML categories any more but the default CSS `display` values. Block elements (`div`, `p`, `h1`, `ul`, `section`, `table`) start on a new line and take the full width; inline elements (`span`, `a`, `em`, `code`, `img`) flow inside a line of text. CSS can change either ([CSS](#css/display)); the content model cannot be changed.
Comments and character references
`<!-- like this -->` is a comment. It is not displayed, but it is sent to everyone who loads the page, so never leave credentials, internal hostnames or "TODO: fix auth" notes in one.
Some characters have a job in markup. To show them as text, write a **character reference**: `&` followed by a name or a number and `;`.

When it is required

in text, whenever a letter, `/` or `!` follows it
to keep `10 ms` or `RT-AX86U Pro` on one line

blocks.out:

blocks.text: The references exist only in the source: once parsed, the DOM holds the plain characters, and `textContent` shows them. Serializing back to HTML (`innerHTML`) escapes `&`, `<` and `>` again. Assigning `textContent` never creates elements, which is the reason it is the safe way to put data into a page ([The DOM](#dom/content)).
How the parser builds the tree

The HTML parser works in two stages. The **tokenizer** reads characters and emits tokens: a start tag with its attributes, an end tag, text, a comment. The **tree builder** takes each token and decides where it goes in the DOM, using a stack of open elements and a long list of rules from the HTML Standard. The rules include what to do with every kind of mistake, so all modern browsers build the same tree from the same broken markup. Nothing makes an HTML parser give up.
For a small status page the result looks like this; Elements shows the same tree, with collapsible nodes.

blocks.code:
document
 └── html  lang="en"
     ├── head
     │   ├── meta  charset="utf-8"
     │   └── title ── "Router status"
     └── body
         ├── h1 ── "Router status"
         ├── p
         │   ├── "WAN: "                     ⟪d:a Text node⟫
         │   └── strong ── "up"
         └── ul  id="clients"
             ├── li  data-ip="192.168.1.50" ── "pi"
             └── li  data-ip="192.168.1.60" ── "nas"

Line by line:

items.text:
A `

`<li>` closes the previous `<li>`. Also legal.

A `

Misnested formatting (`` while `` is open) is handled by the **adoption agency algorithm**: `` is closed inside `` and reopened after it.
Every table gets a `<tbody>` if you did not write one. CSS selectors such as `table > tr` therefore match nothing; write `table > tbody > tr` or just `tr`.
Text directly inside `<table>` is **foster-parented**: moved to just before the table.

blocks.title: Why browsers repair instead of rejecting

blocks.text: In the 1990s browsers competed on showing broken pages, and authors came to rely on it. XHTML tried to make browsers reject malformed pages (one error and the user saw nothing) and lost. HTML5, published in 2014 and now maintained as the living HTML Standard, did the opposite: it wrote down exactly how to recover from every error, so recovery is consistent everywhere. Valid markup is still your job, because a repaired tree is the parser's guess, not your intent.
Semantic elements

A `<div>` means nothing; it is a box for styling. A **semantic element** says what its content is. Browsers turn these meanings into the **accessibility tree** that screen readers navigate, Safari uses them to build its Reader view, and search engines use them to find the main content. They also make your own HTML readable six months later.

`region` (only when it has a name, for example via `aria-labelledby`)

blocks.text: Screen reader users jump between landmarks and headings the way you scan a page with your eyes. On the Mac, VoiceOver ([[⌘F5]] toggles it) opens a list of both with its **rotor** ([[⌃⌥U]]). That makes the heading outline the table of contents of your page: one `<h1>` for the page title, `<h2>` for its main sections, `<h3>` inside those, **never skipping a level** because of how a size looks. Size is CSS's job.

Text, lists and links

**Paragraphs** are `

`. Use `
` only where a line break is part of the content (an address, a poem), and `

` for a thematic break between topics. Whitespace in HTML collapses: any run of spaces and newlines in text renders as one space, except inside `
` or under the CSS `white-space` property.

**Lists** come in three kinds. `<ul>` is unordered (bullets), `<ol>` ordered (numbers; `start="5"` and `reversed` change the counting), and `<dl>` a description list of names and values. Navigation menus are lists of links, so they are usually `<nav><ul><li><a>`.
**Links** are `<a href="...">`. The `href` can be any URL, resolved against the page URL exactly like `new URL(href, location)` in [How the Web Works](#web-intro/urls):

head: `href`
Goes to
rows: an absolute URL on another site
root-relative: same origin, from the top
relative to the current page's directory
the element with `id="clients"` on this page (a fragment)
another page, scrolled to an element there
opens the mail or phone app

blocks.name: <a>
blocks.sum: Create a hyperlink to another page, a place in this page, a file or another app.

how.text: Clicking a link makes the browser resolve `href` against the document's base URL and **navigate**: a new `GET` request, a new document. A link that differs only in its fragment (`#clients`) does not reload; the browser scrolls to the element with that `id` and updates the address bar and the `:target` CSS pseudo-class. Links are focusable with [[Tab]] and activated with [[Return]], which is one reason to use `<a>` rather than a clickable `<span>`.

`target="_blank"` opens a new tab. Current browsers then also apply `rel="noopener"` by default, so the new page cannot script yours through `window.opener`; writing `rel="noopener noreferrer"` makes it explicit and also stops the `Referer` header. `download` asks the browser to save the resource rather than show it (same-origin URLs only). An `<a>` without `href` is a placeholder: not focusable and not a link.

examples.desc: In the Console, list every link on the page with its resolved URL
From Terminal, list the unique link targets of your local site
Find links that open a new tab, then check each has rel set

gotchas: Link text should make sense on its own. Screen readers list links out of context, and a page of "click here" links is useless in that list. Write `device list`.

blocks.text: Images
An image is a void element that points at a file: ``. Four attributes do most of the work.

items.text: **`alt`** is the text alternative, required on every ``. Describe what the image conveys, not what it is: `alt="Router admin page showing WAN up"`, not `alt="screenshot"`. A purely decorative image gets `alt=""`, which tells screen readers to skip it. Leave `alt` out entirely and many screen readers read the file name instead. The alt text is also what appears when the image fails to load.

**`width` and `height`**, in CSS pixels without units, let the browser reserve the right space before the file arrives. Without them the layout jumps when the image loads, a problem measured as **Cumulative Layout Shift**. With them, and CSS `max-width: 100%; height: auto`, the browser keeps the aspect ratio while the image scales.

**`srcset` and `sizes`** offer several files and let the browser pick. With **density descriptors** (`srcset="pi.png 1x, pi@2x.png 2x"`) it picks by screen pixel density, so a Retina Mac gets the sharper file. With **width descriptors** plus `sizes` it picks by the width the image will occupy: `srcset="pi-480.jpg 480w, pi-960.jpg 960w" sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw"`.
**`loading="lazy"`** postpones off-screen images until the user scrolls near them. Never use it on the main image at the top of the page, which should load first.

Then select the first `img` in Elements and run `[$0.naturalWidth, $0.complete, $0.alt]` in the Console; `naturalWidth` is the real pixel width of the loaded file, and 0 for an image that failed.

blocks.sum: Embed an image, with a text alternative, reserved dimensions and optional responsive sources.

how.text: The parser creates the element immediately and the network stack fetches `src` in parallel (images never block parsing or rendering). If `width` and `height` are present the browser derives an aspect ratio and reserves the box at once; the pixels are painted when decoding finishes. `alt` becomes the element's accessible name, and is drawn in place of the picture when loading fails.

With `srcset` the browser chooses one candidate based on device pixel ratio and, with `w` descriptors, on the slot size you describe in `sizes`; `src` is the fallback for old browsers. For different crops or formats per screen, wrap the image in `<picture>` with `<source media="..." srcset="...">` children.

gotchas: `alt` is not a tooltip and not a place for keywords. If removing the image would lose information, describe that information; if not, use `alt=""`.

blocks.text: Tables for real data
Use a table when data has rows *and* columns that mean something, such as a device inventory. Never use one for page layout; CSS grid does that ([CSS](#css/grid)). The structure carries the meaning:

blocks.code:
<table>
 ├── <caption>  what the table is              ⟪d:announced first by screen readers⟫
 ├── <thead>
 │   └── <tr>   <th scope="col"> ...           ⟪d:column headers⟫
 ├── <tbody>
 │   ├── <tr>   <th scope="row"> <td> <td>     ⟪d:a row header, then data cells⟫
 │   └── <tr>   ...
 └── <tfoot>    totals or notes                ⟪d:optional⟫

blocks.text: `<th>` is a header cell and `<td>` a data cell. `scope="col"` or `scope="row"` says which cells a header labels, so when a screen reader user moves to the cell `192.168.1.60` it can announce "IP, nas". `colspan` and `rowspan` merge cells; keep them rare, since they make tables harder to read aloud and to style.

blocks.text: Console drills: `$$('tbody tr').length`; `$$('tbody th').map((th) => th.textContent)` for the names; `$$('tbody tr').map((tr) => [...tr.cells].map((c) => c.textContent))` to turn the whole table into an array of arrays, and wrap that in `copy(...)` to put it on your clipboard as JSON. [CSS](#css) styles this same table properly.

blocks.name: <table>
blocks.sum: Present data in rows and columns, with headers that browsers and screen readers can associate with every cell.

how.text: The browser builds a table model from the rows and cells: every `td` knows its row and column, and through `th` elements (with `scope`, or explicit `headers="id1 id2"` for complex tables) which headers label it. That model is what lets assistive technology read "Status, nas: offline" instead of a lone word. The DOM exposes it too: `table.rows`, `tbody.rows`, `tr.cells`, `cell.cellIndex`.

The parser enforces the structure. A `<tr>` written straight inside `<table>` gets an implied `<tbody>`, and stray text or elements between rows are moved out in front of the table. Column widths are computed from the content of all rows, which is why very large tables render slowly unless CSS sets `table-layout: fixed`.

examples.desc: In the Console, turn a table into an array of objects keyed by the header text

const keys = $$('thead th').map((th) => th.textContent.toLowerCase());
$$('tbody tr').map((tr) => Object.fromEntries([...tr.cells].map((c, i) => [keys[i], c.textContent])));

blocks.text: Forms: how a page sends data

A form is a set of **named controls** plus instructions on where and how to send their values. When the user submits it, the browser runs a fixed algorithm: check the built-in validation rules, collect a list of `name=value` pairs from the controls, encode the list, and send it as a new request to the form's `action` URL. The response replaces the page, as with a link.

blocks.code:
<form action="/register" method="get|post" enctype="...">
   <input name="name" value="printer2">      ─┐
   <input name="ip" value="192.168.1.80">     ├─▶ form data set:  name=printer2
   <input type="checkbox" name="monitor"      │                   ip=192.168.1.80
          checked>                            │                   monitor=on
   <input id="note" value="no name">         ─┘   ✘ skipped (no name attribute)
 </form>
        │ method="get"                    │ method="post"
        ▼                                 ▼
  GET /register?name=printer2&ip=...     POST /register
                                         Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
                                         name=printer2&ip=192.168.1.80&monitor=on

blocks.text: What the browser actually sends

These requests were captured on a small Python server that printed everything it received from Chrome; only the interesting headers are kept. The first form used `method="get"`. The fields were `name`, `ip`, a checked checkbox `monitor`, an unchecked checkbox `alerts`, a `<select name="type">` with *printer* selected, and a `note` containing `2nd floor & hall`:

blocks.code:
GET /register?name=printer2&ip=192.168.1.80&monitor=on&type=printer&note=2nd+floor+%26+hall HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:8822
Referer: http://127.0.0.1:8822/

blocks.text: The same kind of form with `method="post"` puts the identical encoding in the body:

blocks.code:
POST /register HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:8822
Content-Length: 53
Origin: http://127.0.0.1:8822
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

name=printer2&ip=192.168.1.80&note=2nd+floor+%26+hall

blocks.text: And with `enctype="multipart/form-data"` and a file input, each field becomes its own part, separated by a random boundary string, and the file travels as raw bytes with its name and type:

blocks.code:
POST /register HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryLsUJmKUCNRkIHu8x

------WebKitFormBoundaryLsUJmKUCNRkIHu8x
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="name"

------WebKitFormBoundaryLsUJmKUCNRkIHu8x

`method="post"` (default enctype)

blocks.text: GET puts the data in the URL, and URLs end up in browser history, server access logs (like the ones you parsed in [Pipes](#pipes)) and the `Referer` header sent to other sites. **Never send passwords or tokens with GET.** POST is not encrypted either; only HTTPS protects the body on the wire.
Which controls are sent
The browser includes a control in the form data set only if all of these hold. Forgetting one is the most common form bug there is.

items.text: It has a **`name`** attribute. `id` is not enough: `id` is for labels, CSS and scripts; `name` is the key sent to the server.
It is **not disabled** (a `readonly` field *is* sent).
A checkbox or radio button is sent only when **checked**, with its `value`, or `on` if it has none. An unchecked box sends nothing at all, so the server must treat "missing" as "off".
A `<select>` sends the `value` of each selected option (the option's text if it has no `value`); `multiple` repeats the name once per selection.
A submit button is included only if it is the one that submitted the form and it has a name.

blocks.text: You can ask the browser for the exact list it would send: `new FormData(form)` collects it by the same rules (it is covered properly in [The DOM](#dom/forms)), and `URLSearchParams` encodes it.

blocks.text: Every control needs a **label**. Connect them with `for` and `id`, or wrap the control inside the `<label>`. A label is the control's accessible name, and clicking it focuses the field or toggles the checkbox, a bigger target on a phone. A `placeholder` is not a label: it disappears as soon as you type, and it is often too faint to read.

`<fieldset>` groups related controls and `<legend>` names the group, which screen readers announce on entering it; a radio group always belongs in one. A `disabled` fieldset disables every control inside it. The `autocomplete` attribute tells the browser and password managers what a field is for: `username`, `current-password`, `new-password`, `email`, or `off`.

blocks.title: Every button in a form submits it

blocks.text: A `<button>` inside a `<form>` defaults to `type="submit"`. A "Show password" or "Add another IP" button without `type="button"` submits the form and reloads the page, and the bug report says "the page flashes and my input disappears". Give every non-submit button `type="button"`.
A form you can watch

The playground below is a device-registration form. In a real page you would only need the HTML: the browser submits the form and navigates to the server's answer. This playground has no real server, so its 15 lines of JavaScript (explained in [The DOM](#dom/forms)) send the same request with `fetch()` to `/api/echo`, which returns what it received.

blocks.code:
New device 


--- css
label { display: inline-block; min-width: 8em; vertical-align: top; }
input:user-invalid { outline: 2px solid #b00020; }
--- js
// A real browser submits the form itself. This playground has no real
// server, so we build the same request and send it with fetch().
const form = document.querySelector('#reg');
form.addEventListener('submit', async (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  const body = new URLSearchParams(new FormData(form));
  const method = form.method.toUpperCase();
  const action = form.getAttribute('action');
  const url = method === 'GET' ? `${action}?${body}` : action;
  const init = method === 'GET' ? {} : {
    method,
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' },
    body: body.toString(),
  };
  const res = await fetch(url, init);
  document.querySelector('#sent').textContent = `${method} ${url}\n\n` + JSON.stringify(await res.json(), null, 2);
});

blocks.name: <form>
blocks.sum: Group named controls and define where, how and in which encoding their values are sent when the user submits.

how.text: On submission the browser runs interactive validation (unless `novalidate`), fires a cancellable `submit` event, builds the form data set from every named, enabled, checked-or-not-checkable control, encodes it according to `enctype`, and navigates: `GET` appends the encoded pairs to `action` as the query string (replacing any query already there), `POST` sends them as the body. Without `action` the form submits to the current URL; without `method` it uses `GET`.

A submit button can override the form's settings for one submission with `formaction`, `formmethod`, `formenctype` and `formnovalidate`, so a "Save" and a "Delete" button can post to different URLs. Pressing [[Return]] in a text field submits the form through its first submit button. Scripts usually intercept `submit`, call `event.preventDefault()` and send the data with `fetch()` instead, so the page does not reload ([The DOM](#dom/forms)).

Forms cannot send `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE`; only `get`, `post` and `dialog` are valid methods. Use `fetch()` for the others.

blocks.name: <input>
blocks.sum: A single form control whose behaviour, keyboard, validation and value format are chosen by its type attribute.

how.text: `type` picks a whole widget: the on-screen keyboard on phones, the picker, the validation rule and the format of `.value`. An unknown type silently falls back to `text`. Whatever the type, `.value` is always a **string**; number and date inputs add `.valueAsNumber` and `.valueAsDate`. The `value` attribute is only the *initial* value; typing changes the `.value` property, not the attribute, and a reset button restores the attribute's value.

`name` decides whether and under which key the value is sent; `id` connects the label. Constraint attributes (`required`, `pattern`, `min`, `max`, `step`, `minlength`, `maxlength`) feed the browser's validation, whose result you can read in `input.validity` and style with `:invalid` and `:user-invalid`.

how.code: <input type="number" id="port" name="port" min="1" max="65535" step="1" value="22" required>

blocks.name: <label>
blocks.sum: Give a form control its visible caption and its accessible name, and make the caption a click target.

how.text: The browser associates a label with a control either explicitly, when `for` matches the control's `id`, or implicitly, when the control is inside the label. The association does three things: screen readers announce the label text when the field gets focus, clicking or tapping the label focuses the field (or toggles a checkbox), and `input.labels` lists the labels in the DOM.

One label belongs to one control. For a group of radio buttons or checkboxes, label each option and name the group with `<fieldset>` and `<legend>`. When a visible label is impossible (a search field with only an icon button), `aria-label="Search devices"` supplies the accessible name instead.

blocks.text: Built-in validation

The browser can check most input rules itself, before any script or server sees the data. You declare the rules as attributes; the browser blocks submission, focuses the first invalid control and shows a message in the user's language.

head: Attribute or type
Rule
Validity flag set when broken
rows: must not be empty (a checkbox must be checked)
must look like an address or absolute URL
the whole value must match the regular expression
length of text the user typed

blocks.text: Every control has a `validity` object with one flag per rule, and a form's `checkValidity()` returns `false` if any control fails. Reading the flags shows which rule each value breaks:

blocks.page:
<form>
  <input id="name" required>
  <input id="email" type="email" value="admin@lab">
  <input id="email2" type="email" value="admin.lab.local">
  <input id="ip" pattern="(\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3}" value="192.168.1">
  <input id="port" type="number" min="1" max="65535" value="70000">
  <input id="url" type="url" value="router.lan">
</form>

name    ""                 valueMissing
email   "admin@lab"        valid
email2  "admin.lab.local"  typeMismatch
ip      "192.168.1"        patternMismatch
port    "70000"            rangeOverflow
url     "router.lan"       typeMismatch
form valid? false

blocks.text: `admin@lab` passes: the email rule needs only something, an `@` and a host name, because addresses on a local domain are legal. `router.lan` fails the URL rule because it has no scheme, the same reason `new URL()` rejects it.

blocks.title: pattern is anchored and uses the v flag

blocks.text: The browser wraps your pattern as `^(?:pattern)$` and compiles it with JavaScript's `v` (unicodeSets) flag. Anchoring means you never write `^` and `$` yourself. The `v` flag is stricter about character classes: `pattern="[a-z0-9-]+"` is an **invalid** expression there (an unescaped `-` at the end of a class), and an invalid pattern is ignored with only a Console error, so the field silently accepts everything. Write `[a-z0-9\-]+` and check the Console after adding any pattern.

Two more limits. `minlength` and `maxlength` only judge text the user typed, not a value set by the page. And none of this is security: anyone can delete `required` in Elements, or send a request with curl that never touched your form. Client-side validation is for the user's convenience; the **server must check every value again**, as the practice API does when it answers `422 {"error":"ip is not an IPv4 address"}`. To replace the browser's messages with your own, add `novalidate` to the form and use the Constraint Validation API from JavaScript ([The DOM](#dom/forms)). To style fields, prefer `:user-invalid`, which turns red only after the user has interacted with the field, over `:invalid`, which marks an empty required field red before anyone has typed.
id, class and data-* attributes
Three attributes hook HTML up to CSS and JavaScript, and they have distinct jobs.

head: Attribute
Rule
Used by
rows: unique in the document; no spaces
fragment links `#clients`, `<label for>`, `aria-labelledby`, `getElementById()`, CSS `#clients` (very specific, so use sparingly in CSS)
a space-separated list; reusable on any number of elements
any name after `data-`, lower case with hyphens; values are strings

blocks.text: `data-*` attributes keep machine-readable values next to the content they describe, without inventing attributes the browser does not know. In JavaScript, `dataset` converts the names: `data-last-seen` becomes `dataset.lastSeen`, and writing `dataset.checkedBy` creates `data-checked-by`.

blocks.text: A few other **global attributes** work on every element: `hidden` (not rendered, and hidden from screen readers), `title` (a hover tooltip; invisible on touch screens and to many screen reader users, so never the only place for important text), `lang` (for a passage in another language), `tabindex` (keyboard focus, below), `inert` (makes a whole subtree unclickable and unfocusable, handy behind a dialog) and `contenteditable` (lets the user edit the element's text).

Two elements with `id="ip"` produce no error. `getElementById` returns the first, a `<label for="ip">` labels the first, and the second field silently loses its label. When you copy and paste form rows, rename the ids. In the Console, `$$('[id]').map((e) => e.id).filter((id, i, all) => all.indexOf(id) !== i)` lists duplicates.
Accessibility basics

Alongside the DOM the browser builds an **accessibility tree**: for each meaningful element a **role** (button, link, heading, textbox), a **name** (the label or text a screen reader speaks), a **state** (checked, expanded, disabled) and a **value**. VoiceOver on the Mac, VoiceOver and TalkBack on phones, Braille displays and voice control all read that tree, not your pixels. Native HTML elements fill it in correctly for free; most accessibility work is not breaking that.

items.text: **Label every control** with `<label>`, and give icon-only buttons an `aria-label`.
**Give every meaningful image `alt` text**, and decorative ones `alt=""`.
**Use headings in order and landmarks** (`header`, `nav`, `main`, `footer`), so the page can be navigated by structure.

**Use the native element for the job.** `<button>` for actions, `<a href>` for navigation. A `<div onclick>` has no role, is not reachable with [[Tab]], and ignores [[Return]] and [[Space]]; making it equivalent takes `role="button"`, `tabindex="0"` and two key handlers, and it is still worse.

**Use ARIA sparingly.** The first rule of ARIA is not to use it when a native element does the job, and wrong ARIA is worse than none, because it makes the accessibility tree lie. The attributes worth knowing now: `aria-label` (a name when there is no visible text), `aria-labelledby` (name from another element), `aria-current="page"` (the current link in a nav), `aria-expanded` (on a button that shows and hides a panel), `aria-live="polite"` (announce changes to a status line) and `aria-hidden="true"` (hide a decorative icon).

**Keep the keyboard working.** [[Tab]] moves through links, buttons and form fields in DOM order. `tabindex="0"` adds an element to that order, `tabindex="-1"` makes it focusable only from scripts, and positive values reorder the page and should never be used. Never remove the focus outline without providing a visible replacement ([CSS](#css)).

blocks.title: Tab skips links in Safari by default

blocks.text: Out of the box, [[Tab]] in Safari moves only between form fields and pop-up menus; [[⌥]][[Tab]] also stops at links and buttons. To test keyboard navigation as most users experience it, tick **Press Tab to highlight each item on a webpage** in Safari Settings > Advanced, or test in Chrome. macOS-wide, **Keyboard navigation** in System Settings > Keyboard controls whether Tab reaches buttons in dialogs.

Scripts and the head
How a `<script>` element is written decides when it runs, and that decides what it can see and how long the page stays blank.

A classic script that runs in the `<head>` sees an almost empty document, because the parser has not reached the body yet; that is why old tutorials put scripts at the end of `<body>`. The modern default is `<script src="app.js" defer></script>` or `<script type="module" src="app.js"></script>` in the `<head>`: the file downloads while the page parses, and the code runs once the whole DOM exists. Use `async` only for independent scripts such as analytics, which must not depend on other scripts or on the DOM being complete.

Module scripts also run in strict mode, have their own scope instead of creating globals, can use `import` and `export`, and are fetched with CORS, which is why they fail from `file://` ([How the Web Works](#web-intro/origins)). [JavaScript in Depth](#js-deeper) covers modules in detail.
This page proves the order. The "external" script is a `data:` URL standing in for a separate file, because `defer` only works on scripts with a `src`. Read the numbers in the Console.

blocks.code: I come after the first scripts in the source.

blocks.name: <script>
blocks.sum: Load or embed JavaScript, with attributes that decide when it downloads and runs.

how.text: When the parser meets a classic `<script>` it stops, fetches the file if there is a `src`, runs it, and only then continues, because the script could change the document being parsed. `defer` lets parsing continue and queues the script to run, in document order, after parsing finishes and before `DOMContentLoaded`. `async` also downloads in parallel but runs the script the moment it arrives, interrupting the parser briefly, in no guaranteed order. `type="module"` behaves like `defer` by default, and adds strict mode, module scope, `import`/`export` and a CORS fetch.

`integrity` makes the browser verify a hash of the file before running it, which protects you when loading a library from a CDN, and `nomodule` marks a fallback that only browsers without module support run. The element must always be closed with `</script>`, even with `src`, and the text `</script>` cannot appear inside an inline script.

gotchas: `defer` and `async` do nothing on inline scripts. Only `type="module"` defers inline code.
Never put secrets in a script. Every byte of JavaScript is downloaded by every visitor and readable in DevTools.

blocks.text: HTML, XML and checking your markup

HTML looks like XML but is parsed by different rules. The HTML parser is forgiving, case-insensitive, knows which elements are void, and knows more than 2,000 named references such as ` `. The XML parser is strict: every element must be closed or written `<x/>`, names are case-sensitive, attribute values must be quoted, only five named entities exist, and the first error is **fatal**: the browser stops and shows a parse error instead of the page you meant. **XHTML** is the HTML vocabulary written with XML syntax and served as `application/xhtml+xml`, which switches the browser to the XML parser. You will meet XML properly, including how browsers parse it with `DOMParser`, in [XML and Friends](#xml).

Because the parser hides your mistakes, check pages with a **validator**. The W3C's Nu Html Checker at `validator.w3.org/nu` accepts a URL, an uploaded file or pasted text; use upload or paste for pages on `localhost`, which the public service cannot reach. Homebrew packages the same checker for offline use as `vnu` (`brew install vnu`; it depends on Java). It reports errors such as a stray end tag, a `
` inside a `

`, duplicate ids or a missing `alt`, with line numbers. Chrome's DevTools add an **Issues** panel that flags problems such as form fields without labels or `autocomplete` values, and Lighthouse ([Browser DevTools](#devtools)) scores accessibility. A validator checks rules, not judgment: it cannot tell you that your alt text is unhelpful or that a `

` should have been a `
Common mistakes

items.text: **A control without `name`.** It looks and validates normally and is never sent.
**Buttons without `type`.** In a form they submit it; use `type="button"` for everything that is not a submit.

**`
` or `
    ` inside `

    `.** The parser closes the paragraph early and adds an empty one.
**A forgotten end tag on `<b>`, `<i>`, `<a>` or `<strong>`.** The formatting leaks into the following blocks.
**Boolean attributes set to "false".** `disabled="false"` disables; remove the attribute instead.
**Placeholders used as labels.** They vanish on typing and are not reliable accessible names.
**Headings chosen by size.** Choose `h1`-`h6` by structure and style them with CSS.
**Images without `width`/`height` or `alt`.** The layout jumps and screen readers read file names.
**Passwords in a GET form.** They end up in history, logs and `Referer` headers.
**Trusting client-side validation.** The server must re-check every value.
**`table > tr` in CSS or JavaScript.** There is always a `<tbody>` in between.

blocks.title: Audit your own pages from Terminal

task.text: In `~/lab/web`, make sure every page passes three quick checks from Terminal: each `.html` file has a viewport meta tag, no `` lacks `alt`, and no `

hints: `grep -L PATTERN files` lists files that do **not** contain the pattern.
`grep -o '<img[^>]*>' *.html | grep -v 'alt='` shows image tags without alt, each prefixed with its file name.
blocks.solution:
cd ~/lab/web
grep -L 'name="viewport"' *.html
grep -o '<img[^>]*>' *.html | grep -v 'alt='
grep -o '<button[^>]*>' *.html | grep -v 'type='

why.text: Text tools catch the mechanical mistakes in seconds, and `grep -L` inverts the usual question ("which files lack this?"). They cannot parse HTML properly (a tag split over two lines escapes them), which is why the validator is the second step: it runs the real parsing rules and reports structural errors with line numbers.

blocks.verify: cd ~/lab/web && [[ -z "$(grep -L 'name="viewport"' *.html)" ]] && ! grep -o '<img[^>]*>' *.html | grep -qv 'alt=' && echo "OK: viewport everywhere, every img has alt"

questions.q: A form contains `<input type="checkbox" name="alerts" value="email">`, left unchecked. What does the browser send for it?

options.text: Nothing: unchecked checkboxes are left out of the form data set

questions.why: Checkboxes and radio buttons are sent only when checked. The server must treat a missing name as "off".

options.text: An enabled button, because the value is false
A disabled button, because boolean attributes are true whenever they are present
A button that is disabled only in Safari

questions.why: For boolean attributes only presence counts. Remove the attribute (or set the `disabled` property to `false`) to enable the button.

questions.q: Inside a `<form>`, what is the default `type` of a `<button>` without a type attribute?
questions.why: Buttons in a form submit it unless they say `type="button"` or `type="reset"`, a frequent cause of unexpected page reloads.

questions.q: Which script runs after the document has been parsed, in document order, before DOMContentLoaded?
questions.why: `defer` downloads in parallel and runs in order after parsing. `async` runs as soon as it arrives, and `defer` is ignored on inline scripts.

questions.q: An element has `data-last-seen="09:12"`. Which expression reads the value in JavaScript?
questions.why: `dataset` drops the `data-` prefix and converts the remaining hyphenated name to camelCase. `el.getAttribute('data-last-seen')` also works.

terms.def: A node in the DOM built from a start tag, its content and its end tag

The syntax in the source that opens or closes an element, such as

A name="value" pair on a start tag that configures an element
An element that has no content and no end tag, such as img, input, br or meta
An attribute that is true when present and false only when absent, such as disabled or required
A rendering mode that emulates old browser bugs, used when a page has no doctype
The rules for what an element may contain, such as phrasing content only inside p
An escape such as & or → that stands for a character in HTML source
An element that states what its content is (nav, main, table, button) rather than only grouping it
A region of a page (banner, navigation, main, contentinfo) that assistive technology can jump to
The tree of roles, names and states the browser builds for screen readers and other assistive technology
The text assistive technology announces for an element, usually from its label, alt text or content
The list of name=value pairs a form sends: named, enabled controls, with checkboxes and radios only when checked
The encoding of a submitted form body: application/x-www-form-urlencoded or multipart/form-data
